title: 'Leave Iran Now': US Reissues Do-Not-Travel Warning as Tensions Escalate
excerpt: The US Virtual Embassy in Iran issued a fresh security alert on September 21, telling Americans not to travel to Iran "for any reason" and urging those inside the country to leave immediately as the US-Iran confrontation deepens.
body:
• The US Virtual Embassy in Iran issued a fresh security alert on September 21, telling Americans: "Do not travel to Iran for any reason. U.S. citizens should leave Iran now."
  • The alert warns of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions, and says procedures at Iran's land borders could change with little notice.
  • The warning lands amid an escalating US-Iran confrontation — US military and maritime pressure on Tehran, Iranian threats of retaliation, and Iranian-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian airports.
  • Iran remains under the State Department's Level 4 advisory, the highest tier, warning of wrongful detention — especially for dual US-Iranian nationals — and noting Washington has no diplomatic presence in the country.

US Tells Citizens to Get Out of Iran

The United States has renewed its most severe warning for Iran, urging Americans not to travel to the country "for any reason" and telling those already there to leave immediately. The fresh security alert, issued by the US Virtual Embassy in Iran on September 21, warns of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions amid a complex regional security environment.

"Do not travel to Iran for any reason. U.S. citizens should leave Iran now," the alert states. Americans in the region are urged to exercise heightened vigilance and closely monitor developments affecting airports, airlines, and border crossings. The alert also cautions that procedures at Iran's land borders could change with little notice, advising travelers to check the entry requirements of countries they may seek to enter. It adds that US diplomatic facilities — including locations outside the Middle East — have previously been targeted, and that Iran or its supporters could target US interests, businesses, and institutions overseas.

A Confrontation Still Escalating

The alert arrives as the US-Iran confrontation deepens. Washington is maintaining military and maritime pressure on Tehran, while Iranian officials have warned of retaliation against American interests. US Central Command has redirected more than 100 vessels as it tightens a blockade of Iranian ports.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly."

— US Virtual Embassy in Iran, security alert

The alert explicitly cites Iranian-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports — the same thread behind this week's US security alert for government employees in Saudi Arabia.

Diplomacy is running alongside the pressure. Trump is weighing Tehran's terms for ending the war, delivered through Qatari mediators. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, says the terms include ending fighting on all fronts, releasing frozen Iranian funds, and lifting the US naval blockade; Fox News reported seven core demands. Trump cut short a Camp David stay, returning to the White House on Saturday evening, and describes himself as in a "deciding mode" — weighing military action, continued economic pressure, or a deal. He told Fox News that "very big things could happen soon."

What the Alert Changes for Travelers

The renewed warning reinforces that Iran sits under the State Department's Level 4 advisory — "do not travel," the highest category. Its most consequential element is the repeated emphasis on wrongful detention: dual US-Iranian nationals and travelers with any claim to Iranian citizenship face particular risk, because Iran may not recognize US nationality for dual citizens, limiting outside access and complicating consular assistance during a detention.

There is no safety net on the ground: the United States has no embassy or consulate in Iran — Swiss diplomats act as Washington's protecting power — so replacing a lost passport or getting help after an arrest or hospitalization is severely limited.

Even travelers with no intention of entering Iran are affected. Shifting aviation routings around conflict zones and sudden airspace closures have repeatedly disrupted schedules at nearby hubs, raising the chance of last-minute rebooking and extended delays on Gulf connections.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian Americans with family ties in Iran — and the wider diaspora using Gulf hubs — the advisory is a direct planning signal: routes through the region carry growing disruption risk, and anyone with dual US-Iranian nationality faces an acute detention hazard. With India's own trade and cultural stakes in Iran, the diaspora will be watching as both Washington and Tehran signal a decision point is near.

What to Watch

The near-term calendar is crowded. Trump arrives at the UN General Assembly this week, where US Ambassador Mike Waltz says he will make the case that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon. Airlines, markets, and governments across the region will be watching whether Tehran's terms via Qatari mediators draw a response from Washington — and whether the Houthi attacks on Saudi targets widen into a broader escalation. For Americans still in Iran, the message from the US government is unambiguous: leave now, while commercial routes out still exist.
